1235: You refused the night attack. The arrows of Chinzei Hachirō Tametomo reached your sleeping chamber first.
1236: On the night of Hōgen, wait for dawn with too few men.
1237: At the Hour of the Ox, Tametomo and twenty-eight horsemen burst through the east gate of Takamatsu-dono.
1238: His arrows pierced the gate leaves, pierced two men of the Northern Guard, and buried themselves in a pillar of your sleeping chamber. Fire arrows fell on the roof, and the cypress-bark shingles caught at a touch.
1239: Your attendants dragged you from the chamber and out through the west gate. But beyond the west gate stood Yorinaga's soldiers.
1240: By dawn, the Retired Emperor Sutoku at Shirakawa-kita-dono had taken the throne once more. You were sent under guard to Sanuki — the very place to which you had meant to exile your brother.
1241: Afterward you lived nine years by the sea in Sanuki and wrote a great many imayō. Sutoku sent you a sutra scroll copied in his own hand; you looked at it for a long time, then set it as an offering before the Buddha.
1242: You and your brother never saw each other again, not to the day you died.
1243: Historically, Go-Shirakawa's side adopted Yoshitomo's plan for a night attack and took Shirakawa-kita-dono at the Hour of the Tiger on Hōgen 1 (1156), 7th month, 11th day. The Retired Emperor Sutoku was exiled to Sanuki and died there in Chōkan 2 (1164).
1245: You shared a boat with Nobuyori, and Nobuyori capsized it. You lived out your days in seclusion and never again set foot outside Ninna-ji.
1246: Side with Nobuyori in the Heiji Disturbance, and fail to turn your coat in time.
1247: Kiyomori returned. In the battle at the Rokujō riverbed, Nobuyori and Yoshitomo were routed.
1248: Nobuyori fled to you, and you had no way to save him. As they dragged him out, he looked back at you once.
1249: Kiyomori did not kill you — he could not kill a Retired Emperor. But Emperor Nijō's party of direct rule persuaded the Emperor: a Retired Emperor who had conspired with traitors was no longer fit to dwell in the In's palace.
1250: You were sent to Ninna-ji, nominally to take the tonsure and devote yourself to practice. Outside the gate stood soldiers from Rokuhara.
1251: Cloistered rule lasted only a year in your hands. The realm thereafter belonged to Emperor Nijō and Kiyomori. You sang imayō in Ninna-ji for thirty years, and now and then someone came to listen.
1252: When you died, no one called you a tengu. People said only: a Retired Emperor who lost himself in song and dance has died.
1253: Historically, Go-Shirakawa slipped away to Ninna-ji during the Heiji Disturbance and did not conspire with Nobuyori. Afterward he was long at odds with Emperor Nijō; only after Nijō's death in Eiman 1 (1165) was his cloistered rule secured.
1255: You raised troops by In-zen and failed. Kiyomori shut you away in Toba-dono forever.
1256: Defy the Taira openly while your Arms are insufficient.
1258: This time Kiyomori did not hesitate, and there was no Shigemori left to counsel him. You were taken under guard to Toba-dono; a wall rose around it, its top bristling with sharpened bamboo stakes.
1259: Your favourites were beheaded one by one, or exiled to lonely islands of the southern sea. The In's estates were confiscated; the Northern Guard was disbanded.
1260: You lived in Toba-dono for many years. Every spring you watched the cherry blossoms beyond the wall bloom and fall. You began writing on the walls — the words of imayō, one song after another, until all four walls were covered.
1261: Later, someone copied those words down. That is the only complete surviving text of the Ryōjin Hishō.
1262: Those who read the songs in later ages never understood: how could a man imprisoned for half his life write so many joyful songs?
1263: Historically, Go-Shirakawa was confined at Toba-dono after the coup of Jishō 3 (1179), released the following year at the request of the Retired Emperor Takakura, and resumed cloistered rule after Kiyomori's death in Yōwa 1 (1181).
1266: Fourth son of Toba. Ascended the throne as a “stopgap” and held cloistered rule for more than thirty years across five reigns. Devoted to imayō, he compiled the Ryōjin Hishō himself. Yoritomo called him “the Greatest Tengu in Japan.”
1269: Grandson of Shirakawa. After Shirakawa's death he held cloistered rule for twenty-seven years. He called his eldest son Sutoku his “uncle-son” and doted on Konoe, born of Bifukumon-in. His death lit the fuse of the Hōgen Disturbance.
1272: Daughter of Fujiwara no Kinzane and adopted daughter of the Cloistered Emperor Shirakawa. Mother of Sutoku, Go-Shirakawa, Jōsaimon-in and others. She lost her standing when Bifukumon-in rose in favour, and took the tonsure.
1275: Mother of Konoe. Adopted Morihito (Nijō). With Shinzei she drove the decision to enthrone Go-Shirakawa as a “stopgap,” shutting out Sutoku's line.
1278: Enthroned at five, forced to abdicate in favour of Konoe. Defeated in the Hōgen Disturbance and exiled to Sanuki. Remembered as one of the three great vengeful spirits of Japan.
1284: Son of Toba and Bifukumon-in. Enthroned at three, he died at seventeen without an heir. The tale of nails driven into the eyes of the tengu image on Mount Atago arose from his death.
1287: Mother: Minamoto no Yoshiko. Adopted son of Bifukumon-in. On the throne he championed direct imperial rule and stood against his father the In. Died at twenty-three.
1290: Son of Nijō, enthroned at one — the youngest emperor in history. Forced at five to abdicate in favour of his uncle Takakura; died at thirteen.
1293: Mother: Taira no Shigeko. Married Kiyomori's daughter Tokuko. Gentle by nature and a fine flautist. After the Jishō coup he was held in the Taira's grip; died at twenty-one.
1296: Son of Takakura and Tokuko, and Kiyomori's grandson. Enthroned at three, he fled west with the Taira, and at eight went into the sea at Dan-no-ura in the arms of the Nun of the Second Rank.
1300: Fourth son of Takakura. Enthroned without the Sacred Regalia. Gifted in waka and the martial arts, he rose against the shogunate in the Jōkyū War, failed, and was exiled to Oki, where he died.
1303: Brilliant and learned, yet never proclaimed an imperial prince. In Jishō 4 he issued a decree against the Taira as “Prince Saishō”; the rising failed, and he died at Kōmyōzan.
1307: Omuro of Ninna-ji. Learned in Shingon doctrine and in waka.
1310: Chief abbot of Onjō-ji. Killed amid the chaos of the battle at Hōjūji.
1313: Priestess of Kamo. One of the finest women poets of the Shin Kokinshū age, she studied under Fujiwara no Shunzei.
1316: Priestess of Ise; later stood as titular mother to Antoku and Go-Toba.
1319: In his youth Yoritomo served in her household as a chamberlain. After Heiji she was among those who pleaded for his life.
1322: Mother: Lady Tango. She inherited the Chōkōdō's more than 180 estates, becoming the greatest estate holder in the realm.
1325: Daughter of Taira no Tokinobu and half-sister of Tokiko. Clever and beautiful, she was the bond between Go-Shirakawa and Kiyomori. Her death marked the beginning of the rift between the two houses.
1328: Adopted daughter of Minamoto no Arihito. She died soon after bearing Morihito and was posthumously named Empress Dowager.
1331: Daughter of Fujiwara no Kinyoshi. Made Empress after Go-Shirakawa's accession; childless, she later bore the title of Empress Dowager.
1334: First married to Taira no Narifusa, who died after the Jishō coup. She became the one Go-Shirakawa trusted above all in his last years, and her power was immense; people said she was 「女院の如し」 (“like a Nyoin”).
1337: Daughter of Kiyomori, she entered the palace as Go-Shirakawa's adopted child. Mother of Antoku. Rescued at Dan-no-ura, she spent her last years in retreat at Jakkō-in in Ōhara.
1340: After Mochihito's death he fled to Hokuriku and was taken up by Yoshinaka, who pressed hard for his enthronement, in vain.
1343: Father of Tadamichi and Yorinaga. He favoured his second son Yorinaga and was at odds with his eldest, Tadamichi — sowing the seeds of the Hōgen Disturbance.
1346: Lord of Hosshō-ji. He broke with his father and brother and stood with Go-Shirakawa in the Hōgen Disturbance. A master calligrapher, founder of the Hosshō-ji school.
1349: Known as the “Evil Minister of the Left.” Erudite and severe; his diary, the Taiki, survives. Struck in the neck by an arrow in the Hōgen Disturbance, he fled to Nara; his father would not receive him, and he died.
1352: The most learned man of his age; his wife was Go-Shirakawa's wet nurse. He steered the government after Hōgen, reviving the death penalty and the old court rites. In the Heiji Disturbance he had himself buried alive at Tawara and died there.
1357: Go-Shirakawa's wet nurse, later raised to Junior Second Rank.
1359: Provisional Middle Counselor · the In's favourite
1360: High in Go-Shirakawa's favour, he sought command of the Inner Palace Guards and was refused, then raised the Heiji Disturbance with Yoshitomo. When it failed, he was beheaded at the Rokujō riverbed.
1363: Helped Nijō escape during the Heiji Disturbance. Later arrested over the viewing-stand affair and exiled to Awa; recalled, he ended his career as Minister of the Left.
1366: Like Tsunemune, a member of Nijō's direct-rule party; exiled to Nagato.
1369: Son of Tadamichi. Married Kiyomori's daughter Moriko. Died suddenly at twenty-four.
1371: Younger brother of Motozane. Victim of the Denka Noriai incident. Exiled in the Jishō coup; later allied himself with Yoshinaka.
1374: Younger brother of Motofusa. His diary, the Gyokuyō, is the most important source for the age and repeatedly criticizes Go-Shirakawa. Named Regent in Bunji 2 on Yoritomo's recommendation.
1376: Son of Motozane and son-in-law of Kiyomori. Became Kanpaku after the Jishō coup, and stayed in the capital when the Taira fled.
1379: Younger brother of Kanezane. Author of the Gukanshō, which reads Japanese history through the principle of “reason” and calls the age after Hōgen 「武者の世」 (“the age of warriors”).
1381: Provisional Major Counselor · the In's favourite
1382: One of the ringleaders of the Shishigatani plot. Exiled to Bizen, he died there. His sister was Shigemori's wife.
1385: A retainer of Shinzei who, after taking the tonsure, served at Go-Shirakawa's side. When the Shishigatani plot failed he would not yield before Kiyomori; his mouth was torn open and he was beheaded.
1388: Master of the villa at Shishigatani. Exiled to Kikai-ga-shima; when the pardon came he alone was left behind, and he died on the island.
1391: The one who set the toppled jar upright in the jest at Shishigatani. Exiled to Kikai-ga-shima and later pardoned, he compiled the Buddhist tale collection Hōbutsushū.
1393: Poet · Master of the Empress Dowager's Household
1394: Compiled the Senzai Wakashū by Go-Shirakawa's In-zen. Father of Teika; champion of yūgen.
1396: Minister of the Treasury · the In's favourite
1397: Recipient of Yoritomo's “Great Tengu” letter; Yoritomo demanded his dismissal over the Yoshitsune affair.
1400: A skilled drummer. He goaded Go-Shirakawa into breaking with Yoshinaka, and danced with his drum atop the wall during the battle at Hōjūji.
1403: Capable and efficient, he served as go-between for the In and Kamakura, and Yoritomo relied on him heavily. Diary: the Kikki.
1406: Of the Murakami Genji. A favourite of Go-Shirakawa's last years; allied with Lady Tango, he ousted Kanezane in Kenkyū 7.
1409: One of the few permitted to visit Go-Shirakawa during his confinement at Toba-dono.
1412: The first warrior admitted to the palace courtiers' hall. Grew rich on trade with Song China.
1415: Head of the Ise Taira and victor of both the Hōgen and Heiji disturbances. The first warrior to become Chancellor, he developed Fukuhara and the trade with Song. When his grandson Antoku took the throne, Taira power reached its height. He died of fever.
1417: Taira no Tokiko, the Nun of the Second Rank
1419: Grandmother of Antoku. At Dan-no-ura she took the child emperor and the sacred sword in her arms and went into the sea.
1422: After the Heiji Disturbance she begged for Yoritomo's life. For this, her son Yorimori was treated generously by Yoritomo after the Taira fell.
1424: Younger brother of Tokiko. He is said to have declared, “Whoever is not of the Taira is not human.” Exiled to Noto after Dan-no-ura.
1427: Kiyomori's heir. Gentle and steady, he often remonstrated with his father. After his death the Taira broke with the In.
1429: Third son of Kiyomori; head of the Taira after Shigemori's death. Captured at Dan-no-ura and beheaded at Shinohara in Ōmi.
1433: Fourth son of Kiyomori and the bravest of the Taira generals. At Dan-no-ura he said 「見るべき程の事は見つ」 (“All that was worth seeing, I have seen”) and threw himself into the sea.
1435: Middle Captain of the Left Inner Palace Guards
1436: Fifth son of Kiyomori and the general who burned Nara. Captured at Ichi-no-Tani, he was later handed over to the Nara temples and executed.
1438: Middle Captain of the Right Inner Palace Guards
1439: Shigemori's heir, the most beautiful man of his day. Defeated at Fujikawa and at Kurikara. He later took the tonsure and drowned himself in the sea off Kumano.
1442: The young lord at the centre of the Denka Noriai incident. Fell at Dan-no-ura.
1445: A fierce Taira warrior; at Dan-no-ura he leapt into the sea with a Minamoto warrior clamped under each arm.
1448: Younger brother of Kiyomori. When the Taira fled the capital he entrusted his poems to Shunzei. Fell at Ichi-no-Tani.
1451: Nephew of Kiyomori and a fine flautist. Slain at Ichi-no-Tani by Kumagai Naozane, aged sixteen. The Noh play Atsumori tells his story.
1453: Son of Ike-no-Zenni. He stayed in the capital when the Taira fled, and was treated generously by Yoritomo.
1456: Daughter of Kiyomori and wife of Motozane. She administered the estates of the Regents' house; her death sparked the Jishō coup.
1459: Sided with Sutoku in the Hōgen Disturbance and was beheaded by his nephew Kiyomori.
1462: In The Tale of the Heike, she was Kiyomori's favourite until he cast her aside; she then took the tonsure with her mother and sister at Giō-ji in Saga.
1464: In The Tale of the Heike, she supplanted Giō in Kiyomori's favour, then she too took the tonsure and practised alongside Giō.
1467: Sided with Sutoku in the Hōgen Disturbance and was beheaded by his son Yoshitomo.
1472: A hero of the Hōgen Disturbance, rewarded less than Kiyomori. He rose with Nobuyori in the Heiji Disturbance, fled in defeat to Owari, and was killed by Osada Tadamune.
1475: Eighth son of Tameyoshi, peerless with the great bow. After the defeat at Hōgen his sinews were cut and he was exiled to Izu Ōshima; he later took his own life.
1478: Of the Settsu Genji, and a poet. Leader of Prince Mochihito's rising, he took his own life at the Byōdō-in in Uji, aged seventy-seven.
1480: Former Commander of the Right · the Lord of Kamakura
1481: Third son of Yoshitomo. After twenty years of exile in Izu he raised troops in Jishō 4 and founded the Kamakura shogunate. Appointed Sei-i Taishōgun in Kenkyū 3.
1482: Ever mindful of the In's grace
1485: Daughter of Hōjō Tokimasa. Later called the “Nun Shogun.”
1488: Yoritomo's father-in-law. In Bunji 1 he entered the capital with a thousand horsemen and forced the court to sanction the shugo and jitō.
1491: Ninth son of Yoshitomo, by Tokiwa. Three battles, three victories: Ichi-no-Tani, Yashima, Dan-no-ura. Estranged from his brother, he died at Koromogawa.
1495: Sixth son of Yoshitomo; with Yoshitsune, a commander of the western campaign. Later suspected by Yoritomo and exiled to Izu.
1498: Nephew of Yoshitomo. He crushed the Taira at Kurikara and was first into the capital. Ignorant of court ways, he broke with the In and died in defeat at Awazu.
1501: The Tale of the Heike describes her as 「色白く髪長く、容顔まことに優れたり」 (“fair of skin, long of hair, and of surpassing beauty”) — a match for a thousand men.
1504: After Yoshinaka fell at Awazu, he put the point of his sword in his mouth and flung himself headlong from his horse.
1507: Disguised as a yamabushi, he carried Prince Mochihito's decree. Later conspired with Yoshitsune; captured and beheaded.
1510: A serving woman of Kujō-in and the greatest beauty in the capital. After Heiji she fled with her three sons, and later entered Kiyomori's household. Mother of Yoshitsune.
1513: Once a warrior-monk of Mount Hiei. His meeting with Yoshitsune on the Gojō Bridge and his death standing upright at Koromogawa are both later legend.
1516: Captured on Mount Yoshino, she danced before Yoritomo and his wife at Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū, singing of her longing for Yoshitsune.
1518: Saved Yoritomo at Ishibashiyama. Their quarrel over “reverse oars” at Yashima made him Yoshitsune's enemy, and he slandered him again and again.
1521: A court official who came down from the capital to serve as Yoritomo's chief strategist in Kamakura; the shugo-jitō proposal is said to have been his.
1524: The informer who betrayed the Shishigatani plot. Later took part in the battle at Hōjūji.
1527: Slew Atsumori at Ichi-no-Tani. Later took the tonsure as a disciple of Hōnen, under the name Renshō.
1530: At the battle of Yashima he shot down the fan target.
1533: An old retainer of the Minamoto, he killed Yoshitomo in the bath.
1535: Exiled to Izu in Angen 3, he was seized back by the temple monks on the road. Killed by a stray arrow in the battle at Hōjūji.
1538: Born Endō Moritō. Exiled to Izu for a forceful petition at Hōjūji-dono, he befriended Yoritomo there and is said to have urged him to rise.
1542: Travelled to Song China three times. After the burning of Nara he led the rebuilding of Tōdai-ji, introducing the Great Buddha style of architecture.
1545: Born Satō Norikiyo, once of the Retired Emperor Toba's Northern Guard; took the tonsure at twenty-three. In Nin'an 3 he journeyed to Sanuki to mourn Sutoku.
1547: A courtesan of Aohaka in Mino. In her seventies she was brought by Go-Shirakawa to be his teacher, handing down the old style of imayō.
1550: Chinjufu Shōgun · Third lord of the Ōshū Fujiwara
1551: Master of the gold of Hiraizumi and a hundred and seventy thousand horsemen. Protector of the young Yoshitsune.
1553: Fourth lord of the Ōshū Fujiwara
1554: Fearing Yoritomo, he attacked and killed Yoshitsune, and was soon destroyed by Yoritomo all the same.
1557: Officiant at the eye-opening of Tōdai-ji's Great Buddha in Tenpyō-shōhō 4. Four hundred years later, the brush he used was taken up by Go-Shirakawa.
1558: Daiji 2, 9th month: Prince Masahito is born at the Sanjō-Takakura mansion.
1559: Daiji 4: the Cloistered Emperor Shirakawa dies; the Retired Emperor Toba begins cloistered rule.
1560: Eiji 1: Sutoku abdicates in favour of Konoe; the edict names Konoe “Crown Brother.”
1561: Kōji 2: Prince Morihito (Nijō) is born; his mother Yoshiko dies.
1563: Kyūju 2, 7th month: Emperor Konoe dies; Masahito ascends the throne as Emperor Go-Shirakawa.
1564: Hōgen 1, 7th month, 2nd day: the Cloistered Emperor Toba dies. 11th day: the Hōgen Disturbance — Shirakawa-kita-dono falls, Sutoku is exiled to Sanuki, and the death penalty is revived.
1565: Hōgen 2: Go-Shirakawa takes Otomae as his teacher of imayō; Shinzei rebuilds the Greater Imperial Palace.
1566: Hōgen 3, 8th month: abdicates in favour of Emperor Nijō and begins cloistered rule.
1567: Heiji 1, 12th month, 9th day: Nobuyori and Yoshitomo attack Sanjō-dono; Shinzei dies. 25th day: Nijō escapes to Rokuhara.
1568: Eiryaku 1, 1st month: Yoshitomo dies in Owari. 3rd month: Yoritomo is exiled to Izu. 2nd month: Tsunemune and Korekata are arrested.
1569: Ōhō 1, 9th month: Prince Norihito (Takakura) is born to Taira no Shigeko. Hōjūji-dono is completed.
1570: Chōkan 2, 8th month: the Retired Emperor Sutoku dies in Sanuki. 12th month: Rengeō-in (the Sanjūsangendō) is completed.
1571: Eiman 1: Nijō abdicates in favour of Rokujō and dies soon after.
1572: Nin'an 1, 7th month: the Regent Motozane dies; Moriko takes charge of the Regents' house estates.
1573: Nin'an 2, 2nd month: Taira no Kiyomori becomes Chancellor.
1574: Nin'an 3, 2nd month: Emperor Takakura ascends the throne.
1575: Kaō 1, 6th month: Go-Shirakawa takes the tonsure under the Dharma name Gyōshin; Otomae dies. 12th month: the Kaō petition.
